A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material reorganized between versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original multiset and epsilon-tree experiments, synthetic distortion analyses, and SortMPNN/AdaptMPNN results on TU datasets, LRGB, and ZINC12K.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic and benchmark experiments, revises their results, and adds a multiset width experiment and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The core multiset operators and four MPNN architectures remain. However, the ESAN adaptation changes: v1 Appendix I.6 combines node and edge features by addition, with optional subsequent processing; v2 Appendix G.7 instead specifies concatenation, linear projection, and ReLU. This changes a localized part of the procedure.

E1.justification: Both evaluate moment-matched multisets, epsilon-trees, synthetic tuple embeddings, the same five TU datasets, peptides-func, peptides-struct, and ZINC12K. The added width experiment uses the existing multiset construction; smaller network budgets extend configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain their comparator sets: GIN/GCN/GAT for epsilon-trees, GIN/GCN/GraphSage for TU, GINE/GCN/GatedGCN for LRGB, and GIN within ESAN. The new timing comparison uses existing LRGB comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds a width sweep on one eight-element multiset pair, a 1K parameter budget, and timing averaged over 250 epochs. The reported SortMPNN collapse setting for peptides-struct changes from matrix to vector collapse. These are limited protocol/configuration changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure 1 examines how width affects ReLU versus smooth multiset separation. The existing small-model analysis extends to 1K parameters, and Appendix H adds computational-cost analysis. The epsilon-tree distortion plots also revise their ReLU reference exponents. These supplement the retained analyses without substantially expanding their scope.

E5.justification: Both specify stratified 10-fold TU reporting, LRGB reruns with four seeds after tuning, and ten ESAN test seeds, with means and standard deviations. Revised standard-deviation values change results, but the reporting practices and stated run counts remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 3–5 substantially revise the proposed models' results and rankings. AdaptMPNN becomes best on PTC and NCI109; SortMPNN's peptides-struct MAE changes from 0.2494 to 0.2464; its ESAN comparison changes from six wins and one tie against GIN to five wins. Changed LRGB/ESAN settings preclude interpreting all revisions as same-setting gains. Width, 1K-budget, and runtime results are added; Table 2's classification accuracies remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v1's general theorem transferring lower-Hölder guarantees from components to MPNNs is withdrawn, along with the dependent ReluMPNN/AdaptMPNN exponent upper bounds. v2 supplies a width-one ReLU counterexample in Appendix F.2, an explicit upper-Lipschitz proof, and an independent proof of the retained SortMPNN lower-Lipschitz claim in Appendix F.1. This replaces a central mathematical argument.

C1.justification: The headline theoretical scope narrows: v1 Table 1 and Corollary 4.2 advertise guaranteed ReluMPNN/AdaptMPNN exponents, whereas v2 removes those guarantees and leaves relevant lower-stability questions open. SortMPNN's guarantee remains central. The revised introduction also adds robustness to reduced model size to its stated empirical contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains why componentwise expected separation need not transfer to a network: one shared ReLU bias can fail to separate all required multiset pairs simultaneously. It treats wider-ReLU stability as conjectural and AdaptMPNN's epsilon-tree behavior as empirical. It also connects SortMPNN's small-model advantage to width-one stability, materially revising applicability and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-access link, multiset experiment specifications in Appendix G.3, SortMPNN parameter-normalization details, 1K-model widths and parameter counts, and runtime information. These extend an already detailed experimental appendix; newly documented normalization does not by itself establish an implementation change.

R1.justification: The introduction adds connections and citations concerning frames, phase retrieval, group-invariant max filtering, and high-dimensional set representations, including Wang et al. (2024). The central positioning relative to previous sorting methods and MPNN stability research remains. The additional publication entry for 'Towards a bilipschitz invariant theory' represents an already cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around pairwise expected stability and width. Section 4.2 is reorganized around upper stability, failure of general lower-stability transfer, and SortMPNN. Earlier graph-proof appendices are consolidated into Appendix F, norm-equivalence lemmas move to Appendix C, and terminology changes throughout from continuity to stability.

P2.justification: v2 adds the width plot, counterexample diagram, and runtime table; restructures Table 1; extends the budget plot/table; and revises plot labels and reference curves. The document adopts a different template with widespread figure/table reflow, relocated captions, and second-place underlining. The original five figures remain identifiable across renumbering.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is correcting v1's central erroneous MPNN lower-Hölder guarantee, explicitly acknowledged in v2 Section 4.2. The counterexample and independent SortMPNN proof replace an invalid general argument with a more defensible contribution and clearer limits. Added width analysis, timing, and code-access information provide further support. Although the proven scope narrows and benchmark revisions are mixed, the correction substantially improves the paper's scientific reliability.
